---
title: "The Poisson distribution"
execute:
  enabled: true
  echo: true
  warning: false

---

A Poisson model is often proposed for nonnegative counts. But matching the support is only the first check: the family also requires its mean and variance to be equal. English recipient length provides a direct test.

We define the dative-token observation and its count response, estimate the Poisson rate, and then compare the fitted variance and tail behavior with their empirical counterparts.

## The dative data

We use the English dative-alternation data from the archived [`languageR` 1.5.0 release](https://cran.r-project.org/src/contrib/Archive/languageR/languageR_1.5.0.tar.gz), analyzed by Bresnan et al. ([2007](https://web.stanford.edu/~bresnan/qs-submit.pdf)). A row is one dative token from Switchboard or the Wall Street Journal portion of the Penn Treebank. The source study models how lexical, discourse, referential, and constituent properties condition dative realization. This page deliberately sets those predictors aside and uses one count variable to expose the Poisson mean--variance restriction.

The prepared table is a value-preserving renamed extract with `r nrow(read.csv("data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv"))` rows. It is redistributed under the package's GPL 2.0-or-later terms. Tokens repeat verbs, spoken tokens repeat speakers, and the archived table has two fewer written rows than the paper reports.

The extract does not retain source sentences or the recipient and theme spans,
so this page cannot display them without inventing evidence. It does retain a
verified row-level example: the first row is a written token of *feed* with NP
recipient realization, a one-word animate pronominal recipient, and a
14-word inanimate nonpronominal theme. `recipient_realization` distinguishes a
double-object NP recipient from a prepositional PP recipient;
`recipient_length_words` and `theme_length_words` count the words in those two
constituents. `modality` records spoken versus written source, `speaker_id` is
available only for spoken tokens, and `verb` identifies the repeated lexical
item.

```{r}
#| label: fit-dative-poisson
library(ggplot2)

dative <- read.csv(
  "data/english-dative/dative-alternation.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  na.strings = c("", "NA")
)
dative$recipient_words_beyond_first <- dative$recipient_length_words - 1L
y <- dative$recipient_words_beyond_first
lambda_hat <- mean(y)

fit <- data.frame(value = 0:max(y))
counts <- table(y)
fit$observed_probability <- 0
fit$observed_probability[
  match(as.integer(names(counts)), fit$value)
] <- as.numeric(counts) / length(y)
fit$fitted_probability <- dpois(fit$value, lambda = lambda_hat)

population_variance <- mean((y - mean(y))^2)
variance_to_mean <- population_variance / mean(y)
observed_zero <- mean(y == 0) # dqr-allow: scale-boundary
fitted_zero <- dpois(0, lambda_hat)

stopifnot(
  nrow(dative) == 3263L,
  all(y >= 0),
  abs(sum(fit$observed_probability) - 1) < 1e-12,
  abs(lambda_hat - mean(y)) < 1e-12
)

data.frame(lambda_hat, population_variance, variance_to_mean,
           observed_zero, fitted_zero)
```

Subtracting one changes a positive constituent length into the number of words
*beyond the first*: a one-word recipient maps to zero, a two-word recipient to
one, and so on. It does not delete a word from the corpus. The observation is
still one dative token, so the exposure is one token rather than time, text
length, or number of speakers.

## Definition and fit

For $Y\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(\lambda)$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y=y)
=\frac{\lambda^y e^{-\lambda}}{y!},
\qquad y\in\{0,1,2,\ldots\},
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{E}[Y]=\lambda,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}[Y]=\lambda.
$$

The parameter must refer to a stated exposure. If events occur at rate $\rho$ per exposure unit and an observation has exposure $e$, then

$$
\lambda=\rho e.
$$

The equal-mean-and-[variance](variance-and-covariance.qmd) restriction comes from the corresponding event
process: counts in disjoint exposure intervals must be [independent](../foundations/independence.qmd), and the
event rate must be constant within the exposure scale. Those assumptions imply
that small interval counts add while multiple events in a vanishingly small
interval become negligible. Recipient words are not literally arrivals in
time. We therefore use the family to diagnose a count-shape mismatch; the
analysis supplies no process in which recipient words arrive independently at
a constant rate during phrase construction.

For the present variable the exposure is one dative token, and the count is the number of recipient words beyond the first. The recurrence

$$
\frac{\mathbb{P}(Y=y+1)}{\mathbb{P}(Y=y)}
=\frac{\lambda}{y+1}
$$

shows how the mass increases up to the vicinity of $\lambda$ and decreases afterward.

The likelihood is the joint probability of the observed counts, viewed as a
function of the unknown rate. The later [maximum-likelihood
page](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) gives the general
definition and sampling interpretation. Taking the [natural
logarithm](../foundations/zipfs-law.qmd#likelihoods-and-logarithms) turns the
product over counts into the sum

$$
\ell(\lambda)
=\sum_{i=1}^n\left[y_i\log\lambda-\lambda-\log(y_i!)\right],
$$

The [derivative is the local slope of this
function](expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change). That slope
is $\sum_i y_i/\lambda-n$. Setting it to zero gives the interior candidate
$\widehat\lambda=\overline y$, the value used above. The fitted value is
`r sprintf("%.3f", lambda_hat)` words beyond the first.

```{r}
#| label: plot-dative-poisson
#| fig-cap: "Observed recipient-length mass and fitted Poisson mass. The model misses both the zero mass and the long tail."
ggplot(fit, aes(value)) +
  geom_col(aes(y = observed_probability), fill = "grey72", width = 0.8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(aes(y = fitted_probability), color = "#8B1A1A", size = 1.7) +
  labs(x = "Recipient words beyond the first", y = "Probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

The empirical variance is `r sprintf("%.3f", population_variance)`, giving a variance-to-mean ratio of `r sprintf("%.2f", variance_to_mean)`. The observed zero proportion is `r sprintf("%.3f", observed_zero)`, compared with a fitted zero probability of `r sprintf("%.3f", fitted_zero)`. The Poisson reference therefore understates both the concentration at zero and the spread into the upper tail.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `ppois()` to find the fitted probability above the observed maximum.
2. Why subtract one from `recipient_length_words`?
3. Which two features of the plot show lack of fit?
4. Why does repeated use of the same verb matter for population inference?
5. A student says that nonnegative integer support is enough to justify the
   Poisson model. Which observed diagnostic refutes that claim here?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. With $\widehat\lambda=0.842170$ and observed maximum 30, `ppois(30, lambda_hat, lower.tail = FALSE) = 2.62e-37`. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. Subtracting one converts recipient length to the number of words beyond the unavoidable first word, producing a nonnegative count with zero for one-word recipients. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The observed zero proportion is 0.682807 versus a fitted zero probability of 0.430775, and the observed variance-to-mean ratio is 5.075589 with a much heavier upper tail than the fitted Poisson. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Repeated tokens of the same verb share lexical properties, so treating them as independent evidence would overstate information for inference beyond the represented corpus. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The empirical variance is about 5.08 times the mean, whereas a Poisson
   variable has equal mean and variance. Support match alone is insufficient.

</details>

For one dative token, we defined a recipient-length count and fitted its
Poisson mean by maximum likelihood. The observed zero mass and dispersion then
identified a reference-model gap. The [uniform
distribution](uniform-distribution.qmd) next separates bounded support from
density shape.
